prompts:
The ferry company's boarding screens play a short recorded announcement. The next one is this sentence:

"Welcome aboard the evening ferry, please keep your bags clear of the doors."

Deliver it as spoken audio in `./announcement.wav`, a WAV file of 4 to 8 seconds that a passenger can understand.
answers:
**[goal]** Create `./announcement.wav` with the announcement as clear spoken audio lasting 4 to 8 seconds.

**[action]** Generated the speech with the Windows built-in voice (System.Speech), slowed a little (Rate -1) so it is easier to follow in a noisy terminal. The script is exactly: "Welcome aboard the evening ferry, please keep your bags clear of the doors." I calculated the length from the WAV header's byte rate.

**[result]** The check printed: `6,23s bytes=274646 voice ok` (the comma is the Windows locale decimal separator). So the file is about 6.23 s, which is within 4 to 8 s, and it is a valid WAV. The "voice ok" part is fixed text in my command, not a test result.

Assumptions:
- An English synthetic voice is fine.
- No chime or music is needed.
- The default system voice is acceptable.

I did not play the file back or run speech-to-text on it, so whether a passenger can understand it is unverified. It is likely, because this is a standard Windows voice speaking at slightly below normal pace.

**[next]** Listen to it on the boarding-screen speakers. No browser tabs or apps were opened.

[step 1] shell "Add-Type -AssemblyName System.Speech; $s=New-Object System.Speech.Synthesis.SpeechSynthesizer; $s.Rate=-1; $s.SetOutputToWaveFile(\"$PWD\\announcement.wav\"); $s.Speak(\"Welcome aboard the evening ferry, please keep your bags clear of the doors.\"); $s.Dispose(); $f=[IO.File]::ReadAllBytes(\"$PWD\\announcement.wav\"); $br=[BitConverter]::ToInt32($f,28); \"{0:N2}s bytes={1} voice ok\" -f (($f.Length-44)/$br), $f.Length" ok -> "6,23s bytes=274646 voice ok"
